questions.q: What project does this chapter and the Chapter 6 capstone both build on?
options: A small dbt project called retail-orders-analytics, with staging and mart models plus dbt tests
A full e-commerce web application with a shopping cart
A mobile app written in Swift
A video game built in Unity
questions.explain: retail-orders-analytics is the one concrete dbt project this chapter and the capstone use throughout, so every workflow file stays grounded in something real.

questions.q: In the workflow file's `on:` section, what triggers this workflow to run?
options: Every pull request targeting main, and every push directly to main
Only when a repository administrator manually clicks a button
Once per day at midnight, regardless of any code changes
Only when a new GitHub account is created
questions.explain: The `on: pull_request: branches: [main]` and `on: push: branches: [main]` sections define exactly those two triggers.

questions.q: Why does almost every workflow's first step use actions/checkout@v4?
options: Because a fresh runner starts as an empty virtual machine with no code on it at all — checkout clones the repository onto it
Because it installs Python
Because it deletes the repository's history
Because it is required to name the workflow
questions.explain: Without a checkout step, there is no code on the runner for any later step to use — it's an empty Ubuntu machine GitHub just spun up.

questions.q: Why does the workflow pin `python-version: "3.11"` explicitly instead of leaving it unspecified?
options: So the workflow behaves the same today and in the future, instead of silently picking up whatever version Ubuntu happens to default to
Because GitHub Actions cannot run Python at all without a pinned version
Because Python 3.11 is the only version dbt has ever supported
Pinning has no real effect and is purely cosmetic
questions.explain: Pinning a specific version keeps the workflow's behavior stable and reproducible, rather than depending on whatever the runner image defaults to at any given time.

questions.q: Where do you go to watch a workflow run live and read its step-by-step logs?
options: The repository's Actions tab, then into the specific run
The repository's Issues tab
A separate GitHub Actions website unrelated to the repository
The commit message itself
questions.explain: The Actions tab lists every workflow and every run; clicking into a run shows a live, streaming log of every step, with a red X on the exact line that failed.
